questions.stem: What is the solution to T(n) = 2 T(n/2) + Theta(n)?
questions.explanation: Master Case 2: log_b a = 1 = exponent of f. T(n) = Theta(n log n). MergeSort's recurrence.

questions.stem: T(n) = T(n/2) + O(1) solves to:
questions.explanation: Binary search recurrence: log_b a = 0, f(n) = Theta(1), Case 2 with k = 0 gives Theta(log n).

questions.stem: Which Master Theorem case applies to T(n) = 3 T(n/2) + Theta(n)?
questions.explanation: n^{log_2 3} ~ n^{1.585} which dominates f(n) = n, so Case 1 gives T(n) = Theta(n^{log_2 3}). Karatsuba's recurrence.

questions.stem: Karatsuba multiplies two n-digit numbers using how many half-size multiplications?
questions.explanation: Karatsuba's identity reduces 4 multiplications to 3 by reusing (x1+x0)(y1+y0).

questions.stem: What is the role of the 'recursion fairy' in divide-and-conquer correctness proofs?
choices: It is the inductive hypothesis: assume recursive calls return correct answers on smaller inputs
questions.explanation: The recursion fairy is shorthand for the strong induction hypothesis: subproblems return correct results, so you focus on the divide and combine steps.

questions.stem: The combine step in MergeSort takes what time on inputs of total size n?
questions.explanation: Merge is a two-pointer scan; each output position takes O(1), so total work is O(n).

questions.stem: What three cases must be considered in the divide-and-conquer max-subarray algorithm?
choices: Left half, right half, spanning the midpoint
questions.explanation: The optimal subarray is either entirely in the left, entirely in the right, or crosses the midpoint (linear-time suffix+prefix scan).

questions.stem: In the inversion-counting MergeSort, when is a cross-inversion counted?
choices: When an element of L is moved to the output
When an element of R is moved to the output before all of L is exhausted; count is |L| - i remaining in L
Only after both halves are merged
questions.explanation: Each element of R that beats remaining elements of L creates that many new inversions equal to the number of remaining L elements.

questions.stem: Closest Pair of Points runs in what time?
questions.explanation: Standard analysis with pre-sorted lists gives O(n log n); the 2-delta strip's geometric packing argument keeps combine O(n).

questions.stem: Why are only ~7 nearest-y neighbours checked inside the 2-delta strip?
choices: Geometric packing: at most a constant number of points can fit in a 2-delta by delta box at minimum spacing delta
questions.explanation: At least delta-spacing constrains the number of points in any 2-delta x delta box; the packing argument bounds it by a small constant.

questions.stem: If T(n) = 4 T(n/2) + Theta(n^2), what is the asymptotic complexity?
questions.explanation: log_b a = log_2 4 = 2, matching f(n) = n^2. Master Case 2 with k = 0 gives Theta(n^2 log n).

questions.stem: Strong induction is used in divide-and-conquer correctness because:
choices: Subproblems may have size strictly less than n-1, not just n-1
Strong induction is faster than weak induction
questions.explanation: Subproblems can have any size < n. Strong induction allows the hypothesis to apply to all smaller sizes.

questions.stem: Which problem does NOT have a natural divide-and-conquer algorithm in the lecture material?
choices: Single-source shortest paths in a general graph
questions.explanation: Shortest paths use Dijkstra / Bellman-Ford (greedy / DP). The others all fit the divide-and-conquer pattern.

questions.stem: Master Theorem Case 3 requires which extra regularity condition?
choices: a * f(n/b) <= c * f(n) for some c < 1 and large n
questions.explanation: Regularity ensures the combine costs at higher recursion levels don't blow up. Without it Case 3's conclusion can fail.

questions.stem: Karatsuba's running time on n-digit multiplication is approximately:
questions.explanation: T(n) = 3 T(n/2) + O(n) gives Theta(n^{log_2 3}) ~ n^{1.585}.

questions.stem: Which technique is preferred when the master theorem does not apply?
questions.explanation: The recursion tree gives you a per-level cost; summing across levels closes the bound. Substitution then proves the guess.

questions.stem: When does Master Case 1 apply?
choices: f(n) is polynomially smaller than n^{log_b a}
f(n) is polynomially larger than n^{log_b a}
f(n) equals n^{log_b a} up to polylog
questions.explanation: Case 1: recursion dominates because f is asymptotically negligible compared to n^{log_b a}.

questions.stem: What is the height of the recursion tree for T(n) = a T(n/b) + f(n) on input size n?
questions.explanation: Each level shrinks the subproblem size by factor b, giving height log_b n.

questions.stem: Counting Inversions runs in:
questions.explanation: Augmented MergeSort gives the same Theta(n log n) bound.

questions.stem: In the closest-pair algorithm, why is sorting points by y inside the strip important?
choices: To bound the number of nearby candidates to a constant
questions.explanation: After y-sorting, each candidate need only compare to its next ~7 y-neighbours, keeping combine O(n).

questions.stem: T(n) = T(n - 1) + O(n) solves to:
questions.explanation: Sum of O(n) work over n levels gives Theta(n^2). The master theorem does not apply (subtractive, not divisive).

questions.stem: Which divide-and-conquer algorithm fundamentally relies on the integrality of input sizes (no fractional subproblem)?
choices: All of them — recursion always rounds
questions.explanation: Every standard analysis ignores floor/ceiling on n/b; the bounds are unchanged modulo constants.

questions.stem: Why is the combine step's complexity the lever for divide-and-conquer design?
choices: The recurrence's f(n) dictates the case of the master theorem and hence the final bound
It is the easiest step to optimise
It is the only step that runs
questions.explanation: Holding a, b fixed, f(n) is what you control by algorithm design — and it determines whether the answer is Theta(n^{log_b a}), Theta(n^{log_b a} log n), or Theta(f(n)).

questions.stem: For T(n) = 2 T(n/2) + n log n, the solution is:
questions.explanation: Extended Case 2 with k = 1 (f = Theta(n^{log_b a} log^1 n)) gives Theta(n log^2 n).

questions.stem: Which property does NOT hold for divide-and-conquer subproblems?
choices: They are solved independently and combined
questions.explanation: Memoisation/overlap is the DP signature. Divide-and-conquer assumes independent subproblems with no overlapping reuse.
